Dreams in Tolstoy's Anna Karenina

Robert Mollinger PHD

Robert Mollinger

77 Charles Street
New York, N.Y. 10024

Robert Mollinger   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is on the faculty of National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysts and is author of Psychoanalysis and Literature: An Introduction.

Dreams play an important role in Tolstoy's Anna Karenina (1875-77). Tolstoy opens the novel with Oblonsky's dream of a dinner party, and he highlights several climactic scenes with the dreams of Anna and Vronsky. For example, Anna reports a recurrent dream at the beginning of her adulterous involvement, and both she and Vronsky report similar dreams during the period she is pregnant, a pregnancy which eventually forces an open break with her husband Karenin. However, these dreams have not been examined from a psychoanalytic perspective. Such an examination can both reveal the personalities of the characters, who are presented as real people in a “realistic” context, and, in consequence, deepen our understanding of the novel.

When working with the dream of a fictional character, the psychoanalytic literary critic is under certain limitations. He cannot focus on what the psychoanalyst would in working with a patient's dream. For instance, transferential feelings, step-by-step associations of the dreamer, and past and current analytic material do not exist in the literary work. However, much of significance remains. In terms of the dream's emotional context, one of the foremost guidelines used in interpretation, the dream in a novel is dreamt and reported at a particular point in the action, after particular events have occurred, and at a time when the character may be grappling with a particular emotional concern.

This timely book marks the emergence of psychotherapy as a potent weapon in the all out war against cancer, the number two killer disease. Goldberg, the editor, has organized 17 chapters by 19 authors in five sections, starting with theory and ending with group and family treatment.

As recently'as 1965, a paper* drew this response from a physician: “We may not even dare think of emotional factors in cancer at our institution.” And this from a surgeon: “Even if you proved it for the next ten years, I wouldn't believe it.” But despite the conservative politics of cancer, the book affirms that it is no longer heresy to see the importance of emotions in a disease regarded as the most organic of all organic diseases.

In a sensitive foreword, Hyman Spotnitz touches on similarities in the personality features of schizophrenic and cancer patients and predicts a more widespread use of psychotherapy in the treatment of cancer. The survival function of psychosis during cortisone treatment of serious organic diseases has been described by the reviewer elsewhere. There is an apparent reciprocal relationship between schizophrenia and cancer: they seem mutually incompatible. Mailer's phrase, “Cancer is madness denied,” is clinically valid.

Verny's book takes us on a psychic journey into the depths of human development. He demonstrates, with passion, the unequivocal significance of intrauterine life by presenting the unborn child as a feeling, remembering, and responding being. Verny's work is revolutionary in that it challenges all of our previous notions of intellectual and emotional development and introduces us to an, until now, seldom imagined alternative. The foundation of his work is simply, “What happens after birth is an elaboration of, and depends on, what happened prior to it.” From this premise we follow Verny through an extraordinary investigation of the child's life in utero.

The book begins by providing some basic facts, not unfamiliar to the general public, regarding precautions every woman should take into consideration during pregnancy, e.g., the effects of smoking, alcohol consumption, and poor nutrition on the unborn child. However, Verny goes further to suggest that not only physiological factors, but psychological ones, as well, may have a tremendous impact on the unborn, and consequently, may produce certain emotional (and physical) predispositions for neuroses, manifested after birth. Drawing on findings from all areas of science he provides compelling examples to support his hypotheses regarding mother-child prenatal communication and comes to some enlightening conclusions concerning the far-reaching importance of the prenatal experience. For example, it is Verny's belief that there exists a direct correlation between maternal disposition toward pregnancy and the biological susceptibility of the fetus. Thus, he prescribes the formulation of a strong intrauterine bond (along with suggestions on how to accomplish this) between mother and child as the best protection against the outside world's dangers and uncertainties.

General Discussion

Audience: I have a question for Dr. Spotnitz. Something was said about therapists actually driven to suicide by patients. I wanted a little more detail. It seems inconceivable.

Spotnitz: You want to know how a therapist is driven to suicide?

Audience: Yes.

Spotnitz: I will tell you one story. I was working in my office with a group and one of the ladies said, You know, my therapist wants me to have a suicide pact with him. I went to him for a couple of years and then I seduced him. We had an affair; I left my husband and he's leaving his wife. He wants me to live with him and then to kill ourselves. He doesn't think we can go on living in the present situation.

He betrayed his family. She betrayed her relatives. They have both been isolated. She asked me what she should do. You heard Dr. Sternbach say you have a right to make suggestions, so I made a suggestion. I said, Never see him again. She never saw him again, and two weeks later he killed himself. Audience: What happened?

Spotnitz: What happened to whom?

Audience: The therapist.

Alex Bernstein

Alex Bernstein  

“Paradoxical interventions” are much in the air now. They have been discovered, for example, by The New York Times, which recently devoted an article to the methods of the Milan group headed by Mara Selvini Palazzoli. They have, however, long been used by therapists under varying conditions, and have an even longer history in other areas. Japanese labor disputes have long been characterized by the use of paradoxical tactics (strength through weakness). For example, striking Japanese railroad employees would lie down on the tracks in front of an oncoming train to force the train to stop; this tactic of weakness was responded to by a management counter maneuver, which consisted of the engineer slowing the train to a crawl, jumping off and running alongside, yelling to the striker that he was now incapable of stopping the train; which was further responded to by the strikers' having themselves tied down so that they could not move, thereby forcing the engineers (who could see the strikers' condition) to jump back onto the train and stop it! Each of these maneuvers was intended to force the other side to make a move by exploiting their perception of one's own helplessness.

This is the nub of paradoxical interventions. You take an action (counting speech as action, of course) which has a clear apparent goal in order actually to achieve its opposite.

For psychotherapists, the questions are: with what kind of patients, and under what conditions, should or can paradoxical interventions be used? What kind of paradoxical interventions are there? And when should they be avoided?

Gerald Weeks and Luciano L'Abate offer, in their new book, at least the beginnings of answers to these questions.

Psychoanalytic Explorations of Technique: Discourse on The Theory of Therapy. Harold P. Blum, Editor, New York: International Universities Press, 1980, 468 pp.

June Bernstein

June Bernstein

June Bernstein  

The modifications of technique that may be required for the treatment of narcissistic patients strike many of the contributors to this collection as inconsistent with what they understand by psychoanalysis.

According to Blum, the editor, “Interpretation leading to insight is the specific and most powerful agent of the psychoanalytic curative process.” Since children and immature adults are developmentally restricted in their ability to employ insight and to profit from interpretation, he doubts whether the treatment employed for them can properly be called psychoanalysis.

Anna Freud and Hansi Kennedy agree that lack of insight is characteristic of children. Kennedy says that with children the analytic work goes hand in hand with the developmental process itself, and that intellectual insight plays a small part in the therapeutic results. Anna Freud notes that lack of insight in young children taxes the therapist's ingenuity and introduces the need for technical modifications which decrease with the age and maturity of the child.

Among the various contributors, Neubauer stands out by asking: “Does our clinical experience teach us that those patients who have achieved a stable and organized insight are those who have been cured?” He remarks that one view is that insight may be a byproduct of the analytic process, but that it is the process itself, not insight, that is therapeutic.

Introduction

H. R.

H. R.

H. R.  

The seven books reviewed in this issue focus on four topics: destructive impulses, narcissistic disorders, feminism, and therapeutic technique.

Two new books with a psychoanalytic orientation discuss the death wish in unfamiliar contexts.

The review of Nathan Schwartz-Salant's book on narcissism by Jonathan J. Goldberg discusses parallels between the Narcissus myth, clinical phenomena and the prevalence of narcissistic character disorders as illustrative of Jung's idea of evolution within the archetypes. On the subject of narcissistic disorders, June Bernstein reports the positions staked out by leading classical psychoanalysts in the collection of essays edited by Harold P. Blum. She finds them theoretically astute, but lacking new approaches to treatment. Marie C. Nelson defends Jule Eisenbud's hypothesis that paranormal foreknowledge is a form of thought transference. The patient aims his death wish at others by means of psychokinetic influences. Whether the outcome is the foretold disaster depends, as in the case of conscious goals, on what opposing factors arise. Equally unusual are Velikovsky's extensions of Freud's idea of the compulsion to repeat unconscious racially inherited memories. As reported by Deborah Margolis, Velikovsky fears that our present destructive technology makes possible the repetition of traumas the human race suffered when we survived pre-historic natural catastrophes.

Opening Remarks

Nathan Schwartz-Salant

Nathan Schwartz-Salant

Nathan Schwartz-Salant  

It is my great pleasure to welcome you to the Yearly Scientific Conference of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis. I am Nathan Schwartz-Salant, NAAP's president for the past year, and I will be moderating today's discussions. NAAP is in the unique position of bringing together diverse points of view about psyche. Today our topic is the borderline patient, and it is difficult to imagine a subject that could better benefit from diverse points of view! Like the alchemical Mercury it continually eludes being caught and contained, and when captured seems to always escape. How often do we read in the literature of the same school of thought that so-and-so is dealing with a different kind of borderline patient than I am?

Today we bring together proponents of the Adlerian, Freudian and Jungian points of view. That alone is quite an accomplishment! To think of these three names under the same roof, speaking about the same clinical issues is perhaps a small step towards healing the splitting in our own profession and group psyche. “Physician heal thyself” goes the ancient maxim, and if we are to attempt to heal the borderline patient, or our own borderline aspects, perhaps we must also address the splits in our larger community of psychoanalysis. NAAP attempts to do this.

responseSet.abstract:

Editor's Introduction

Jane Goldberg

Jane Goldberg

Jane Goldberg  

The Editors have chosen articles for this issue of Modern Psychoanalysis which demonstrate the application of psychoanalytic principles to disciplines other than a therapeutic analysis of patients.

Freud introduced the concept of wider application in The Interpretation of Dreams by an analysis of the characters of Hamlet and Oedipus. Freud's discovery of the fictitious nature of his patients' childhood memories freed him from a narrow dependence on fact. Distinctions, then between fact and fantasy blurred, and works of art—literature, painting, and sculpture—became vehicles for exploration of psychoanalytic, if not factual, truth.

In defending what was then called “lay” analysis in 1926, Freud emphasized that analysts need not come from scientific or medical backgrounds, and that they need not limit the application of their theory to patients, the mind of the artist or their work. He stated that analysts with backgrounds in virtually any field can be trained and psychoanalytic theory applied to a wide variety of endeavors.

As that idea has come to be increasingly accepted in this country, we reap the benefit of the creative thinking of more individuals from more diversified backgrounds. The willingness of analysts to apply their analytic tools to the other disciplines and professions has given us an understanding of these fields previously not available. It is the enthusiasm with which this marriage has been made that enables us to produce this issue.

Thomas Hardy's two comments about The Return of the Native have contributed to a critical misreading of that novel. First, in a letter to Arthur Hopkins (his illustrator for the serialized version appearing in Belgravia in 1878), Hardy cryptically ranks the characters: “‘The order of importance of the characters is as follows: 1. Mrs. Yeobright.’”* Second, in a note added to the sixth book of The Return of the Native in April 1912, Hardy seems to cast doubt upon that book's artistic integrity: He admits that “certain circumstances of serial publication” forced him to devise a happy ending in the form of a marriage between Thomasin and Venn.** Critics have followed Hardy's lead, naturally enough, by both ignoring Mrs. Yeobright's indomitable influence, not only on Clym's character but on the structure of the plot as well,† and by persisting in their view of the Book Sixth as a mistake, an excrescence, or a “comic epilogue.”‡

Psychoanalysis has not, in recent years, fared well in the burgeoning field of feminist scholarship. Objections have been made to various notions of Freud and his proteges; among them, penis envy, female masochism, the vaginal (as opposed to the supposedly less mature and pre-genital clitoral) orgasm, and to the emphasis on intrapsychic conflict rather than situational, cultural, sociological and environmental factors in the formation of personality. That Freud's theories may be limited by their embeddedness in a particular culture is scarcely disputed by the most ardent of classical analysts. Flexibility in organizing, extending, and even revising the original theory has been demonstrated by a number of individual analysts, and by whole schools of analytic thought.

This book brings together many papers of major importance in the field of family therapy that have been published in the last twenty-five years and includes thoughtful commentaries by the editors.

Divided into two sections, the first dealing with theory and the second with practice, the book offers an eclectic view of the basis of family problems, from Bateson's celebrated double-bind paper of 1956, to the Vogel-Bell paper on the scapegoat, to Lidz's view of schizophrenia as stemming from unhealthy family constellations and treatable by the isolation of the patient from the family (by treating the family first without the patient and then with the patient, in conjunction with individual treatment for the patient).

Deborah Margolis

Deborah Margolis

Deborah Margolis  

“Those who do not remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” This dictum, first enunciated by the philosopher George Santayana, is the theme of Immanuel Velikovsky's book, Mankind in Amnesia. In this posthumous work Velikovsky, psychoanalyst and scientist, draws upon Freud's insights as underpinnings for his theme. When an individual, says Freud, experiences an event, a thought, or a feeling too fearsome

234

to tolerate, he gets rid of it by repressing its memory into the unconscious. The repressed, however, is never quiescent. This unruly resident of the unconscious finds derivative ways to emerge into daylight, whether through emotional or somatic symptoms, or through the blind repetition in a new guise of the original experience that led to the repression. Freud called this phenomenon the repetition compulsion. Giving the theory of repression a global cast, Freud further postulated that present day man suffers from unconscious guilt feelings, not only as a result of his personal experiences, but also for acts committed and guilt feelings experienced by primeval man in the remote past. The fearsome act, the memory of which the caveman pushed into his unconscious, was patricide, the killing of the father by his sons so that they might possess the women of the tribe. Freud postulated a racial unconscious which is imprinted with the guilt feelings of our primeval forebears and which continues its enduring presence in the individual unconscious even to this day. Every son, says Freud, is destined to go through the Oedipus complex and to experience the guilt feelings engendered by his unconscious wish to do away with his father and possess his mother, as well as the guilt feelings harking back phylogenetically to primeval man and universally experienced through the ages.

“If we consider mankind as a whole,” Velikovsky quotes Freud, “and substitute it for a single individual, we discover that it too has developed delusions which are inaccessible to logical criticism and which contradict reality. If, in spite of this, they [the delusions] are able to exert an extraordinary power over men, investigation leads us to the same explanation as in the case of the individual. They owe their power to the element of historical truth which they have brought up from the repression of the forgotten and primeval past.

I am a professional musician, a concert pianist, teacher, composer and author of teaching materials. In the Fall of 1972 I enrolled at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and remained there for four years. While my original intention was to become an analyst, it became clear to me that analytic training was far more meaningful to me in the context of my professional music activities, particularly teaching. In this article I shall attempt to describe ways in which modern analysis has influenced my teaching.

The Initial Interview

I find that many people, whether children or adults, experience some anxious feelings at the initial interview and are particularly uneasy about being asked to play the piano. In fact, the traditional initial interview for music lessons is usually, at least in part, an evaluation of the prospective student by the teacher; if the teacher is seeking only markedly talented or experienced students some candidates are bound to be rejected.

In order to deal with this anxiety, I generally suggest to the students that our first interview is for the purpose of exploring whether we can work out a suitable arrangement and, above all, whether I am the most suitable teacher for their needs.

I would like to discuss what modern psychoanalysis has contributed to the understanding of childhood and adolescent development. There is a modern analytic body of theory which has grown out of analytic investigation, but when we train analysts, we train them to enter the analytic room with an open mind to a particular patient. Psychoanalysis developed first as a method of investigation, then as a technique for treatment, and finally as a science of the human mind. Most of our study of child development is done through observation and participation in the regression of particular patients on the couch. If a patient allows himself to enter this process, he regresses to his earliest childhood and he offers us the experience of going back with him to get in touch with our own infantile feelings. So, it is on a very personal level that we learn how children develop. One of the most important things for the analyst to know is his own early development through the experiences he has with his patients.

To begin this discussion I'm going to take you back to the first few months of life, after the dawn of awareness, but prior to the development of cognition. When the patient has regressed to this period of his life, pleasure and pain are all he knows. That is, the infant is aware of sensory experiences only.

This book is a quite wonderful weaving of the mythological and the clinical perspectives as applied to the interpretation of narcissistic character disorders, the focus of much recent psychoanalytic attention. Rich in case material and specific illustrations, Schwartz-Salant's study shows also how inadequate a merely diagnostic perspective is to an understanding of the phenomenon of narcissism. Clinical data and phenomena, as psychoanalysts like Kernberg and even Kohut fail to understand, are only partial manifestations of an entire mythic structure. Similarly, individual version of myths, like Ovid's of the Narcissus story, are always only selective retellings of larger tales, as is Freud's version of the Oedipus story, onesided though illuminating. As Monahan indicates in his preface, this monograph reflects the work of many years research into the problem of the clinical prediction of violence. These 134 pages are packed with a truly daunting number of studies, facts and critical examinations of this difficult problem.

From the first chapter Introduction to a Controversy, in which

248

Monahan discusses the difficulty of predicting violence while stressing the moral and political issues raised by such predictions, he engages his reader. The interface of the law and the mental health profession is of growing importance. It is the rare mental health professional who can afford to be unaware of the issues raised by Monahan.

Monahan builds a strong case for combining skills in clinical prediction with statistical approaches to improving clinical prediction. Knowledge and use of the actuarial correlates of violent behavior greatly increases the ability of the mental health professional to predict violence. Monahan makes the point that the single most important predictor of violence is the base rate of violence in the population from which the patient is drawn.

Because Monahan sees violence as an interaction between the perpetrator and his environment (including the people in his environment), he stresses the need for more research into this interaction. Indeed, he sees this as the primary avenue for increasing reliability of predictions of violence in the future.

Finally, Monahan repeatedly states his belief that the mental health professional should not assume the burden of deciding what is to be done with a client's life in forensic cases. The mental health professional should state the facts as clearly as possible. It is the law which must decide how these facts are to be used.

This monograph is well worth reading even by those who are not involved in forensic work.

Assigned to teach an eight week remedial writing skills course, I experienced feelings of dread over the possibility of finding myself saddled with a group of angry students out for revenge. At best, poorly skilled high school students might view such a course as a boring-but-safe rehash of grammar-cum-formula-writing on nonvital topics. As the school setting in which I worked was one that encouraged experimentation, I got a wild idea. How about making the course a simulated business? Each student could be an “employee” and, rather than class, we'd have “staff” meetings; the writing/learning tasks could evolve from this context. I wanted a business that would provide a range of gratifying “jobs.” The thought occurred to me, how about a resort hotel? The idea became a plan as I realized what it would communicate to the students, namely my acceptance and understanding of their emotional level, for remedial students seem invariably narcissistic and infantile in development, and the plan would encompass their need for fantasy, fun, and gratification with a gradual, titrated exposure to the frustrations of learning. I could be a good teacher without repeating stale and ineffectual methods with a resistant group. And I could have fun.

When class convened for the first meeting, I told the group of fifteen youngsters (fourteen of them black, residents of Harlem) of this plan and gave them their first assignment: to think of a name for the new corporation.

Editorial Introduction

This issue is dedicated to the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis.

When, following a history of strife within the profession, Jordan Packer arrived in New York late in 1972 with an idea for a national psychoanalytic organization, it seemed almost too optimistic to believe that the various schools within the field could cooperate. Yet, ten institutes were represented at a meeting in Los Angeles in 1973 to plan the formation of NAAP and an annual conference.

A committee, appointed to determine what training was available nationwide, contacted each training facility in the country. Twenty-seven institutes were invited to the second annual conference.

Early conferences were devoted to establishing an organization and to determining suitable standards for accreditation in psychoanalysis. By the third annual conference, some Freudians were expressing concern about accepting Freudian, Jungian and Aderlian training under one title, and an attempt was made to re-establish separation within the profession. The danger of falling into a repetition of past history was averted by a decision to continue in an ecumenical spirit, healing the wounds inflicted by subgroups on one another.

Alex Bernstein

Alex Bernstein

16 Gerlach Place

Alex Bernstein   Computer consultant who has long been interested in artificial intelligence. In 1957 he wrote the first chess playing computer program, and has published on the artificial evolution of problem-solving machines. He is in training at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies.

The function of science is to explain and predict. Scientists observe the world around them, gather the facts, and develop theories. What tests is a theory supposed to pass in order for it to become generally accepted? The theory must explain how a system works, and must incorporate all known facts about that system. The theory must be simpler than a previously accepted theory, for given two theories, both of which explain the same phenomena, a scientific principle holds that the simpler theory (being more probable) is better. Lastly, for a theory to be more than just descriptive, it must be able to predict events. It is this predictability that makes a successful theory. So, Einstein predicted from his theory that light waves were subject to gravitation and later observation confirmed this theory.

Yet, despite these stringent conditions, and despite the reputation for infallibility that has grown around science, there is a skeleton in science's closet. The skeleton is that no scientific theory has yet lasted. Why is this? It is because scientific theories are inductive—they are constructed to explain a set of known facts—they are not developed, as are mathematical proofs, out of the deductive process, going from the general to the particular (which is always true)—and as new facts are discovered, new theories are needed.

Audience: Did you indicate that there is some age distinction in the borderline patient? Is age a factor?

Shulman: Yes, in the sense that with increasing age a good many people are going to learn some of the social skills that they do not yet have. Learning social skills will allow them to start getting positive feedback from the group. Age is a factor also in seeing the borderline as a developmental phase rather than an eventual diagnostic category. When we begin to see the symptoms of a psychosis or some other chronic illness, we generally make that diagnosis rather than the diagnosis of borderline personality.

Audience: Are different kinds of interventions used with the borderline patient than with other patients in Adlerian technique?

Shulman: There are some modifications of the usual interventions. The amount of encouragement, of positive feedback from the therapist, is exceedingly important. I cannot use irony with the borderline the way I might with the more mature neurotic patient because the borderline will take it as a hostile rather than as a humorous comment. On the other hand, just plain encouragement and acceptance without bringing some very important aspects of reality into the therapeutic picture will simply permit the therapist to go on being the idealized external image-object and no problem solving will take place. It is important, as Kernberg points out, to interpret the defensive behavior when the patient gets angry, I often treat it as if the patient is frightened rather than angry, and I will say directly to the patient, What's upsetting you, what's frightening you? instead of, What's making you angry? I feel that sometimes you pass by the anger and get right to the fear that way. I won't let the borderline do something impulsive if I can help it. I will say directly, Don't do that. Discussion Following Dr. Levene's Address

ELlenbogen: Dr. Levene compared a number of criteria that Dr. Shulman talked about and mentioned fragments of discussions with friends he considers normal or normal-neurotic. But he did not deal with other items Dr. Shulman mentioned, people who are constantly anti-social, who are manipulative, who get into fights, who are alcoholic, who are impulsive, who use no critical thinking, who make no decisions at all. Now, is he saying these things do not exist? Or are there other categories or what? I am confused about his answer to those things.

Levene: I think there are mensches in the world and I think there are people who hang out in bad places. I do not think we necessarily have to give them a diagnosis. I do not think that Kernberg would agree with the diagnosis of borderline just put on alcoholism, drug abuse, or anti-social behavior. There are people who are criminals, and if you want to look at criminals, look at their opposites, people who are cops. Cops and robbers play an interesting game. They each play both sides of an archetypal equation. I mistrust both sides. If you want to see splitting and over-idealization, just look at our relationship with other countries, our willingness to use nuclear bombs to stand up to them. That is what I am worried about: unambivalent rage. There are people who hang out in prisons, there are prisoners and there are the imprisoners. I do not necessarily think that a diagnosis such as borderline, or trying to figure out exactly the month of life when they chose that particular mode, is helpful. The substance of my paper is that all of us have criminal elements in us. Our whole country acts in criminal ways. Each of us has polymorphous perverse attitudes. We do not just look and screw in the missionary position. A fully healthy person has fluidity in his consciousness. He feels his ambisexuality, he experiences his homosexuality or her homosexuality. He may even live it out at one time or another.

Discussion Following Dr. Spotnitz' Address

Schwartz-Salant: Oscar Sternbach, our Freudian discussant, has published widely on various subjects with special attention to problems of sado-masochism. He is known for such works as: Sex Without Love and Marriage Without Responsibility and The Pursuit of Happiness and the Epidemic of Depression. He is a widely-respected psychoanalyst. We are privileged to have Oscar Sternbach to offer his comments on Dr. Spotnitz's presentation in the context of the history of psychoanalytic technique from Freud to the present.

Oscar Sternbach, Discussant: Borderline conditions are not disorders which are well circumscribed and definable by certain symptoms or by a definite etiology or by a definite course. There is in fact nothing definite in these conditions, certainly not a definite therapy or a certain technique of handling them. For some time, it seemed that the only thing certain was that they would not respond or they would respond negatively to so-called classic analytic technique. Kernberg (1979) assures us that even that is not certain, but I think borderline conditions owe their present popularity in psychoanalysis to the fact that they make it justifiable to drop classic analytic technique.

To say somebody has a borderline condition is like vaguely saying he is mentally not quite stable, his ego does not function as it should. The borderline and narcissistic patient is often simply designated difficult. His ego does not function normally. One or more important ego functions, affect control, impulse control, integrative capacity is not normal. Borderline conditions were first mentioned after World War II. These malfunctions were described as very serious deviations, but as time went on the concept became more inclusive, until recently Ganzarain (1982) could say: “We are all borderline.” Historically, the concept was preceded by the “preoedipal condition” and followed by the “narcissistic pathology,” all of which are similar.

Marie Nelson

Marie Nelson

Marie Nelson  

Based on the rigorous exploration of precognitive phenomena occurring in his psychoanalytic practice, Dr. Eisenbud undertakes a systematic inquiry into the therapeutic, scientific and philosophical issues involved in this aspect of psi and arrives at a set of postulates that offer valuable guidelines for future investigators and in so doing help to account for the massive resistance by organized science to the generous inventory of well-documented and witnessed reports existing in the field.

A scrupulous researcher and scientific thinker in his own right, with a lifetime of professional experience as a psychoanalyst and a parapsychologist, this latest volume consolidates the author's seminal ideas regarding the least explicable area of parapsychology: foreknowledge. At the outset he differentiates between dreams involving true foreknowledge, cognition of an event prior to its occurrence, and dreams of pseudo-foreknowledge, cognition of an event that has occurred, albeit without the patient's knowledge; for example, an event reported in a newspaper that was printed but not yet on sale prior to the dream. This, on the ground that only true foreknowledge cannot be accounted for by any means presently known to science.

One of the fascinating and rewarding aspects of this work is the double vision it provides. For the reader of Shakespeare, this collection of psychoanalytic criticism offers a stunning variety of insights into the characters of the plays, into the revelations provided by examination of language, and ultimately into the mind that fathered it all, that of the author himself.

More particular to the analyst is the vision provided in the other direction, the opportunity to see other minds at work in what are finally case studies in whole or part, with sharp interpretations of specific language and thought that has been spread out before the critic for his consideration by the creative mind.

By utilizing developments in analytic thought since Freud, Jones, and other initial literary analyst-critics, the writers here bring to bear the contribution of people like Erikson, Mahler, and Winnicott to broaden and deepen the worth of psychoanalytic criticism in a notable selection of essays.

Freud and Women. Lucy Freeman and Herbert Strean. New York: Frederick Ungar Publishing Co., 1981

A. P.

A. P.

A. P.  

This volume discusses Freud's relations with women in his personal and professional life and how they influenced the development of his theory of sexuality.

Freud's mother believed that he was destined for fame and gave him the feeling about himself that fostered greatness. Freeman and Strean suggest that perhaps Freud's competition with his sisters prevented him from acknowledging that if a

249

girl has been the indisputable favorite of her mother, she, too, can keep for life “the confidence of success that induces real success.”

Freud's childhood desire to know all his mother's thoughts and feelings seems to have led him to make the request of his wife that she tell him all of her thoughts and feelings. This same request of his patients would, of course, become a cornerstone of “the talking cure.” However, the authors state, “One of Freud's limitations as a therapist, which emerged particularly in his work with Helene Deutsch, was his reluctance to help patients feel the hatred which they transferred toward him from their parents.”

The authors believe “that the defensive operations he used to protect and preserve his idealized vision of his mother from invasion by his deep hostility toward her left their mark on his theories of psychosexual development and on his notions of womankind. He loved and cherished women, but he also feared them and, at times, showed contempt for them. Thus, his unresolved ambivalence toward women affects several of his psychoanalytic theories of feminity.”

Freeman and Strean go on to say that “he was the one to point out the power of ambivalence, the mixed feelings of love and hate that exist in all of us. In Freud's life, his love and respect for women far outweighed his repressed hatred.”

The authors suggest that Freud showed women the way to sexual and emotional freedom, thus leading the way to emancipation.

Modern Psychoanalysis of Learning in the Classroom

William Kirman PHD

William Kirman

310 East 65th St.
New York, N.Y. 10021

William Kirman   NAAP certified psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He is Chairman of the Department of Guidance and Counseling at Long Island University and a faculty member and a training analyst for the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He is the author of Modem Psychoanalysis in the Schools.

The teacher striving toward cooperative classroom learning would do well to emulate a parent with a well functioning family as a model. During a child's growing years parents provide the emotional ingredients necessary to meet unfolding maturational needs as well as the intellectual stimulation important for acquiring skills and basic knowledge of the world around him. Both of these tasks are accomplished in a social milieu called the family, where cooperative functioning of parents and children complements and makes possible the meeting of the child's emotional and intellectual needs. Likewise, the classroom student must be provided with the appropriate learning experience in an atmosphere conducive to optimal intellectual and emotional functioning.

Learning modalities

The communication of cognitive material in the classroom remains a primary goal of the teacher, since it is not desirable to produce emotionally mature but intellectually deficient students. Accordingly, the teacher must become clearly attuned to the varying ways in which students learn. For each individual the road to significant learning may follow a different path. No single educational philosophy can adequately be used to unlock all doors to learning.

Modern Psychoanalysis as Philosophy

Howard Ruttenberg PHD

Howard Ruttenberg

32 West 82nd St.
New York, N.Y. 10024

Howard Ruttenberg   Professor of philosophy at York College, City University of New York. He is currently in training at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies.

Any problem becomes a philosophical one when pushed to an extreme by an inquirer reflecting on his assumptions and methods. Thus Freud (1925) began as a scientist who became a physician for financial reasons, but, as a result of his efforts to treat mental illness, he also became a philosopher with a new conception of human nature. This in turn enabled him to relate the limited practical aims of the physician to the inclusive aim of human happiness and the means and prospects of attaining it that are the traditional domain of the philosopher. Philosophy means love of wisdom, and wisdom is that knowledge of the nature of things that reveals at the same time the basis of the good life. Freud's inquiries took him beyond the natural sciences to art, morals, and politics, but he makes it clear (Freud, 1916) that for him all of these are part of a general science of nature. His “wisdom” follows Copernicus in denying man a unique place in the universe that symbolizes our supposed non-natural, spiritual connection with God. His “wisdom” follows Darwin, who made the distinction of the human species to consist in the complexity of a nature evolved from simpler forms of life, by tracing the evolution of the human individual and race to the interplay of simple drives. In discovering the neuroses, Freud extended the explanation by necessary, natural causes to all of human life. Modern psychoanalysis (Spotnitz, 1969)

An Adlerian Interpretation of the Borderline Personality

Bernard Shulman MD

Bernard Shulman

2913 North Commonwealth Ave.
Chicago, Illinois 60603

Bernard Shulman   Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at North-western University Medical School and Chairman of the Department of Psychiatry at St. Joseph Hospital in Chicago. He is immediate past President of the International Association of Individual Psychology, an instructor and training analyst at the Alfred Adler Institute of Chicago and contributor to Adlerian theory and practice.

Schwartz-Salant: Bernard Shulman has published many papers on Adlerian psychology addressing diverse clinical issues in treatment of individuals and groups. He has made important contributions to our understanding of schizophrenia and the affective disorders, as well as such topics as dreams, sexuality, and psychiatric aspects of headaches. Among his latest publications is a book, co-authored with Forgus, entitled Personality Theory, a Cognitive View. His work lately is focused on the idea of personality styles and deals with personality factors in bipolar affective disorders. Dr. Shulman thus brings to us a rich psychiatric background. He is president of the International Association of Individual Psychology, and among other positions is a professor of Psychiatry at Northwestern Medical School. It is a great pleasure to introduce Bernard Shulman to you.

Michael Stone (1980) has recently pointed out that the borderline personality has been studied from at least three different points of view: as an attenuated form of psychosis (Kety et al, 1968); as a syndrome (Grinker et al, 1968; Gunderson and Singer, 1975); and as a level of functioning (Kernberg, 1980; Masterson and Rinsley, 1975; Rinsley, 1981). Some symptoms resemble affective disorders (Akiskal, 1981), some seem to indicate some organic brain dysfunction (Andrulonis et al, 1981).

He is honorary president of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, and author of numerous publications, among them, The Couch and the Circle: A Story of Group Psychotherapy; Modern Psychoanalysis of the Schizophrenic Patient: Theory of the Technique; Psychotherapy of Preoedipal Conditions: Schizophrenia and Severe Character Disorders; and co-author of Treatment of the Narcissistic Neuroses. It is a great pleasure to have Dr. Spotnitiz with us today.

When Freud first worked with patients, he was treating psychoneurotics. They had oedipal problems. Patients with oedipal problems have a supergo and an ego and an id, all well organized in their minds. Freud's patients had the capacity to a greater or lesser extent to love the truth. Freud also loved the truth. They worked together to understand the problems of the human mind and their own personal problems. Freud primarily interpreted what was going on between them. So interpretation became the classical method of treating psycho-neurotic patients.

As time went by, you all know, the psychoneurotic patient seems to have disappeared.
